key_facts: Thickened, itchy eczema on the face, scalp, neck and backs of hands in an older man, sparing the upper eyelids, behind the ears and under the chin.
Extreme sensitivity to UVB, UVA and sometimes visible light, behaving like contact allergy to an endogenous light-altered antigen; contact allergy is common alongside.
Strict photoprotection (including visible light), emollients, potent topical steroid or tacrolimus; refer for phototesting and patch testing; specialist immunosuppression.
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and drug photosensitivity as mimics; erythroderma.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A **chronic, persistent, often severe eczema of sun-exposed skin** caused by abnormal sensitivity to UVB, often UVA and sometimes visible light. Typically affects **older men (60+), usually fair-skinned**, in the UK; also seen in younger people with darker skin types and in people with longstanding atopic eczema. Older synonyms: persistent light reaction, photosensitive eczema, actinic reticuloid (severe pseudolymphomatous end of the spectrum).

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Thought to be a **delayed-type hypersensitivity (allergic contact-type) reaction to an endogenous skin antigen photo-modified by UV** — i.e. "photo-allergy to one's own skin". Strong links with **contact allergy**: up to ~3/4 have positive patch tests, especially to **Compositae (sesquiterpene lactones — chrysanthemums, daisies, dandelions)**, fragrance, colophony, rubber chemicals and **sunscreen filters**. May follow a photoallergic drug reaction (persistent light reaction) or airborne contact dermatitis. Cumulative sun damage and outdoor work/gardening/hobbies in older men are risk factors. Some drugs (thiazides, certain antibiotics) can aggravate it.

ul: **Itchy, red, thickened, lichenified eczematous plaques** on face (forehead, cheeks, nose), scalp in bald men, ears, **back and sides of neck, V of chest, dorsal hands/forearms**.
**Sharp cut-off** at collar and wrist/cuff; **sparing** of upper eyelids, skin creases, behind/under ears, under chin, finger webs (DermNet gallery).
Can extend to covered sites and progress to **erythroderma** in severe cases.
Present year-round but worse in summer; patients may say even indoor light/fluorescent light triggers flares.
Darker skin: hyperpigmentation and lichenification more than redness.
Severe: infiltrated papules/plaques with atypical lymphocytes (actinic reticuloid) — mimics cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome).
**Monochromator phototesting** (photobiology unit): reduced minimal erythema dose to UVB ± UVA ± visible — confirms diagnosis and guides photoprotection.
**Patch testing and photopatch testing** (Compositae mix, fragrance, sunscreen agents, plant extracts).
Biopsy: chronic spongiotic dermatitis ± atypical lymphoid infiltrate; exclude lymphoma (Sézary cells, T-cell receptor gene studies if erythrodermic).
Bloods: ANA/ENA (exclude lupus), porphyrins; HIV in younger patients with new severe photosensitivity.
Drug history (exclude drug photosensitivity).

ddx.name: Airborne contact dermatitis (e.g. Compositae, sawdust)
ddx.f: Involves **shaded** sites too (upper eyelids, under chin, behind ears); patch tests; may coexist with CAD

ddx.name: Photoallergic drug reaction
ddx.f: Temporal link to drug; resolves after stopping (persistent light reaction = CAD-like evolution)

ddx.name: PMLE
ddx.f: Younger, intermittent, clears within weeks, not lichenified

ddx.name: Rosacea
ddx.f: Central face, papulopustules, telangiectasia, flushing; no eczema

sections.title: Management
blocks: **Refer to dermatology** (phototesting/patch testing are specialist). While waiting and long-term:

ul: **Rigorous photoprotection** (UVB, UVA ± visible): broad-spectrum SPF 50+ high UVA, **fragrance-free**, ideally **mineral/tinted** if visible-light sensitive or sunscreen-allergic; wide-brimmed hats, long sleeves, gloves, UV-protective window film; avoid sun 10:00–16:00.
**Allergen avoidance** per patch tests (e.g. Compositae plants in garden, fragrance).
**Emollients + soap substitutes.**

**Topical corticosteroids** — potent to body/hands; moderate short courses to face; **topical calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus 0.1%/pimecrolimus — off-label for CAD, specialist-guided) as steroid-sparing on the face. Counsel: TCIs can cause transient burning; strict sun protection while using them.
Flares: short oral prednisolone (prescriber decision).
Specialist systemic: **azathioprine**, ciclosporin, mycophenolate, methotrexate, dupilumab (case reports); low-dose PUVA/narrowband UVB under steroid cover (hardening) in selected patients.
**Vitamin D supplementation** (10 micrograms daily, or check levels) because of strict sun avoidance.
Review **aggravating drugs** (thiazides, etc.).

refer.t: Erythroderma or rapidly spreading eczema: same-day dermatology.
Persistent photosensitive eczema in an older adult: refer for **phototesting and patch testing**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Erythroderma or rapidly spreading eczema: same-day dermatology.
Persistent photosensitive eczema in an older adult: refer for **phototesting and patch testing**.

blocks: Suspected CAD → routine dermatology (photobiology). **Urgent** if erythrodermic, systemically unwell, lymphadenopathy or atypical infiltrated plaques (exclude lymphoma).

pearls: "Eczema in an older man that is worst on the face, neck and backs of hands — and spares behind the ears" = think CAD.
Patients may be sensitised to their **own sunscreen** — choose fragrance-free, minimal-filter or physical products and ask about reactions.
Gardening is a double hit (UV + Compositae): gloves, long sleeves, avoid chrysanthemums/daisies if allergic.
Severe disease can be life-limiting (house-bound): signpost BAD leaflet and support; consider mental health.
Many improve over years with strict avoidance.
